core: what a survey is (structured set of questions to many people)
good question craft (clear, neutral, one idea at a time)
question types (open-ended, rating scales, multiple choice)
pitfalls (leading, double-barreled, response bias, low response rates)

claims.claim: A UX survey is a tool that gathers information about users' feelings, thoughts, and behaviors related to a product or service, typically as a set of questions given to many participants.
Quantitative surveys count how many people give each answer; as Nielsen Norman Group puts it, they measure how many say they do this or that, rather than measuring behavior directly.
Good survey questions are clear and specific enough that every respondent can answer, are neutral so they do not imply a particular answer or give away expectations, and ask only one thing at a time.

Questions that ask respondents to evaluate more than one concept at once are known as double-barreled questions; they are difficult to answer and often lead to responses that are difficult to interpret.

Open-ended questions let respondents answer in their own words, while closed questions restrict them to a limited set of possible answers; in surveys, closed questions often take the form of multiple-choice or rating-scale items.
Every extra survey question reduces the response rate and makes the results more suspect, so keeping surveys short helps people finish them.

Survey response biases can come from survey fatigue, respondents' lack of understanding, leading words, and question order; researchers counter them with clear unbiased questions, randomized question order, and pilot tests with a small audience.

Answer options shape answers: in a 2008 Pew poll, 58 percent chose the economy when it was offered as a listed option, while only 35 percent of respondents answering in their own words volunteered it.

sourceRecords.title: 28 Tips for Creating Great Qualitative Surveys
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: quantitative surveys count how many people say they do this or that; write neutral questions that do not imply particular answers or give away expectations; every extra question reduces response rate and decreases validity, so keep surveys short; test surveys with colleagues and a small set of testers from the target audience. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Open-Ended vs. Closed Questions in User Research
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: open-ended questions allow free-form text answers and encourage exploration; closed questions restrict respondents to a limited set of possible answers; in surveys closed questions often take the form of multiple-choice or rating-scale items; closed questions can become leading when they suggest an answer. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Surveys (UX Surveys) — What are UX Surveys?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: definition of UX surveys as tools gathering information about users' feelings, thoughts, and behaviors, typically a set of questions; response-bias countermeasures (clear unbiased questions, randomize order, pilot tests, mix of question types); surveys' drawbacks including biased responses from fatigue and limits on behavioral detail. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Writing Survey Questions
sourceRecords.notes: Reputable survey-methodology authority (Tier C). Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports: question writing as the most important part of the survey process; clear and specific questions; double-barreled questions named and defined; open- vs closed-ended distinction with the 2008 election issue example (58% vs 35%); randomizing answer order to spread order bias; even accurate random sampling is wasted on ambiguous or biased questions. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
